newsitem.title: USA: Clinton polishes State of the Union speech.
newsitem.headline: Clinton polishes State of the Union speech.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Tuesday prepared to deliver a State of Union speech laying out his plans to maintain peace and prosperity, with improving America's educational system as its centrepiece, aides said.

"The centrepiece of the speech will be a specific agenda for the future of American education," White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters. "He's working on the speech and it's shaping up quite well."
In an annual tradition mandated by the Constitution, Clinton was to deliver his overview of the state of the nation to Congress in a televised speech scheduled for 9 p.m. EST (0200 GMT on Wednesday).
Clinton, previewing the speech on Monday in remarks to state governors, focused on a time-tested state-of-the-union theme that America is strong but faces many challenges.

"The nation is strong, we are at peace, we have extraordinary prosperity," Clinton said. "But ... there are significant challenges which if not faced will have destructive consequences for our nation in the years ahead."

Aides have said Clinton would call for addressing three pieces of "unfinished business": balancing the budget, making last year's welfare reform law work and reforming the system by which the country finances political campaigns.
Beyond these matters, McCurry said Clinton will be putting his emphasis on education.
"The president I expect ... will say that his top priority when you think about how you prepare Americans for the future ... is the quality of America's education," he said.

McCurry said the Democratic president, who began a second four-year term on Jan. 20, would propose new initiatives to expand health care coverage for millions of children, fight juvenile crime and rid U.S. schools of illicit drugs.

Clinton also planned to discuss how to carry out a new welfare law ending a 61-year guarantee of federal aid to the poor, and to try to take the steam out of a Republican drive for a Constitutional amendment requiring a balanced budget.

"The president will certainly talk about the importance of balancing the budget and talk about his budget plan to do it, and he'll suggest that we ought to do it and get on with that business," McCurry said.
He added that Clinton would tell the country that a budget amendment "is a moot question" if Congress and the president get together and balance the budget by a certain date.

Clinton's report is required by the Constitution, which says the president "shall from time to time give to the Congress information of the State of the Union, and recommend to their consideration such measures as he shall judge necessary and expedient."

A Republican response was to be delivered by Representative J.C. Watts of Oklahoma, a former college football player who is a rising political star and one of that party's few nationally prominent blacks.
